lesson.title: ESS: Stitching Many Access Points into One Network
lesson.summary: An Extended Service Set links multiple basic service sets through a wired distribution system so that a whole building or campus appears to clients as a single, continuous wireless network they can roam across.
lesson.body:
A single access point, forming one BSS, only covers a limited physical area, maybe a few thousand square feet, with walls and interference cutting that down further in practice. Real buildings, and certainly campuses, are far larger than that, and worse, people carrying laptops and phones actually move around while staying connected, walking from a lobby into an elevator into an office on another floor. A wireless architecture that forced a fresh manual reconnection every time someone changed rooms would be unusable, so Wi-Fi defines a way to stitch many BSSs into one logical network: the Extended Service Set, or ESS.

An ESS is formed by connecting the access points of two or more BSSs to a shared distribution system, almost always ordinary wired Ethernet running through the building's switches, and configuring every one of those access points with the identical SSID and identical security settings. Structurally, each access point still runs its own independent BSS with its own unique BSSID, exactly as described in the BSS concept, but because they share one SSID and one backend wired network, client devices experience them as a single continuous network rather than as separate ones to be joined and rejoined.

This is what makes roaming possible. As a client physically moves and the signal from its current access point weakens while a neighboring access point's signal strengthens, the client's Wi-Fi radio decides to disassociate from the first AP and associate with the second, keeping the identical SSID and, ideally, the identical IP address and any active connections, so applications like a video call barely notice the handoff. The wired distribution system is what makes this transparent: because all the access points are bridged onto the same wired backbone, traffic addressed to the client's MAC address simply starts arriving through whichever access point the client is currently associated with.

Take the three floor office building from the access point example, three APs, one per floor, all configured with SSID OfficeNet and all wired into the same building switch. An employee starts a video call at their desk on floor one, associated with the floor one AP's BSS. They then walk to a meeting room on floor three. As they move, their laptop measures the floor one AP's signal weakening and the floor three AP's signal strengthening, and at some point re-associates with the floor three AP, still under the same SSID, OfficeNet. Because both access points sit on the same wired distribution system and the laptop keeps the same IP address, the video call continues through the handoff, often with only a brief, barely noticeable interruption.

The quality of that handoff, how brief the interruption is, depends heavily on how the access points are configured and how much coverage overlap exists between neighboring BSSs, which is a large part of why network planners think carefully about channel assignment and AP placement, the subject the next concept, Wi-Fi channels, addresses directly.
